title: Moms and Babies Not Being Heard: UK Promises Big Changes
summary: Imagine going to the hospital to have a baby and the doctors and nurses don't listen to you. A new report says that's happening to too many women in England. The report, by Baroness Valerie Amos, found that women and babies are being failed "on a scale that shames our society." That means it's so bad it should make everyone feel embarrassed. Racism and discrimination are "embedded throughout the system" — meaning they're a deep part of how things work. Health Secretary James Murray said new rules for emergency maternity care will come out this week. The government will also create 1,000 temporary midwife jobs (midwives help deliver babies) and spend £41 million to fix old maternity buildings. But some families are disappointed. The Birth Trauma Association said the report is a "huge missed opportunity." They say it didn't include enough of what women told Baroness Amos, like injuries from forceps (a tool used in some births) and the stress that can follow a difficult birth. Another expert, Donna Ockenden, who investigated bad maternity care in Nottingham, said one person can't fix the whole system alone. The government hopes these changes will start to make things better, but many people think there's a long way to go.
why_it_matters: This shows how important it is that doctors and nurses listen to patients and treat everyone fairly—something you might see when you visit a hospital yourself.

Related to pregnancy and the time when a baby is born.

questions.question: According to the report, how serious are the problems in England's maternity care?
options: a) They make the country feel proud.
b) They are a shameful failure.
c) They are getting better very fast.
d) Nobody really notices.
questions.correct_answer: b) They are a shameful failure.

questions.question: Who is the Health Secretary that promised new emergency care rules?
options: a) Baroness Valerie Amos
b) Donna Ockenden
c) James Murray
d) The Birth Trauma Association

questions.question: What did the government plan to do to help maternity care?
options: a) Close several hospitals
b) Create 1,000 temporary midwife jobs
c) Stop all use of forceps
d) Ask the royal family for advice

questions.question: Why did the Birth Trauma Association call the report a 'huge missed opportunity'?
options: a) It left out many women's real experiences.
b) It made doctors look too bad.
c) It talked only about Scotland.
d) It spent too much money.
questions.correct_answer: a) It left out many women's real experiences.

questions.question: According to the article, what are forceps?
options: a) A kind of medicine
b) A tool used in some births
c) A special hospital bed
d) A type of bandage
questions.correct_answer: b) A tool used in some births

questions.question: What did Donna Ockenden say about fixing the maternity care system?
options: a) One person can easily fix it.
b) The system is already working well.
c) One person cannot fix the whole system alone.
d) Only doctors should fix it.
questions.correct_answer: c) One person cannot fix the whole system alone.

background_read: The UK's National Health Service (NHS) provides free hospital care for everyone, including when women give birth.
Baroness Valerie Amos (a former politician who now works on fairness and equality issues) led the team that wrote this report.
In England, midwives are specially trained nurses who care for women during pregnancy and help deliver babies.
Article_Structure: WHO: Pregnant women, families, Baroness Valerie Amos, Health Secretary James Murray, the Birth Trauma Association, Donna Ockenden

WHAT: A damning report shows deep failings in maternity care, with embedded racism and discrimination; the government announces new rules, 1,000 midwife jobs, and £41 million for repairs, but campaigners say key problems were ignored.
WHY: Because a report revealed shameful levels of neglect and unfair treatment, forcing officials to act, yet families feel the response still misses many of their most painful experiences.

perspectives.description: They see this as an urgent chance to fix maternity care by hiring more midwives and upgrading old buildings, hoping these steps will protect mothers and babies better.
They feel let down because the report did not fully include what many women said, like injuries from forceps or lasting emotional stress, and worry the changes won't go deep enough.
They argue that the system is broken across many levels and that one person or one set of rules cannot fix everything; real change needs many parts working together.
